stem: A client develops wheezing, lip swelling, and a rapid weak pulse within minutes of eating a cookie containing nuts. Which hypersensitivity reaction is most consistent with this presentation?
rationale: This is an immediate allergic reaction with airway and cardiovascular symptoms, which fits IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity. Type IV reactions are delayed and T-cell mediated, while types II and III involve antibody-mediated cytotoxicity or immune-complex deposition.
source: Immune/inflammation study guide; hypersensitivity PowerPoint text; saved immunity and practice exam quizzes

stem: Which white blood cells are classified as lymphocytes? Select all that apply.
rationale: Lymphocytes include B cells, T cells, and natural killer cells. Neutrophils and basophils are granulocytes, so they do not belong in the lymphocyte group.
source: Immune/inflammation study guide; saved immunity quiz

stem: A client has difficulty swallowing a large capsule, so the nurse checks whether the medication is available as a liquid. Which medication right is the nurse primarily applying?
rationale: Changing from a capsule to a liquid formulation addresses the route/form of administration so the medication can be given safely. Dose, time, and documentation remain important, but they are not the main issue in this stem.
source: Foundations in Pharmacology study guide; medication safety PowerPoint text; saved mixed quiz

stem: A client with heart failure has dyspnea, cough, tachycardia, and crackles in the lung bases. Which side of heart failure do these findings most strongly suggest?
rationale: Left-sided heart failure causes blood to back up into the pulmonary circulation, producing dyspnea, cough, crackles, and tachycardia. Right-sided failure more often produces systemic venous congestion such as peripheral edema and neck vein distention.
source: Cardiology study guide; cardiovascular pathophysiology PowerPoint text; saved cardiovascular quizzes

stem: A client starts lisinopril for hypertension. Which teaching point is most important for the nurse to include?
options: Report swelling of the lips, tongue, face, or trouble breathing immediately.
Take an extra dose if blood pressure remains elevated after 1 hour.
Use potassium-containing salt substitutes freely to lower sodium intake.
Stop the medication once blood pressure readings are normal.
correctAnswers: Report swelling of the lips, tongue, face, or trouble breathing immediately.
rationale: ACE inhibitors can rarely cause angioedema, which can threaten the airway and requires urgent care. Potassium salt substitutes can increase hyperkalemia risk, and the medication should not be self-adjusted or stopped without provider guidance.
source: Cardiology study guide; cardiac meds PowerPoint text; saved cardiovascular pharmacology quiz

stem: A cardiac monitor shows a heart rate of 130/min with a sawtooth waveform. Which rhythm should the nurse suspect?
rationale: A sawtooth atrial pattern is characteristic of atrial flutter. Atrial fibrillation is typically irregularly irregular, and PVCs or ventricular tachycardia originate from ventricular rhythms rather than a sawtooth atrial pattern.
source: Cardiology study guide; antiarrhythmic PowerPoint text; saved cardiovascular quizzes

stem: Which statement best describes ventilation?
options: Movement of air into and out of the respiratory tract
Exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide across the alveolar membrane
Blood flow through the pulmonary capillaries
Oxygen use by cells to produce energy
correctAnswers: Movement of air into and out of the respiratory tract
rationale: Ventilation is the movement of air in and out of the lungs. Diffusion is gas movement across the alveolar-capillary membrane, and perfusion is blood flow through the pulmonary circulation.
source: Pulmonary study guide; respiratory pathophysiology PowerPoint text; saved respiratory quiz

stem: A client with asthma is having acute wheezing and shortness of breath. Which medication should the nurse expect to use first for rapid relief?
rationale: Albuterol is a short-acting beta-2 agonist used for rescue bronchodilation. Fluticasone, salmeterol, and montelukast are used for control or maintenance rather than immediate relief of acute bronchospasm.
source: Pulmonary study guide; respiratory treatment PowerPoint text; saved mixed and respiratory quizzes

stem: Which adverse effects should the nurse include when teaching about first-generation antihistamines such as diphenhydramine? Select all that apply.
rationale: First-generation antihistamines commonly cause anticholinergic effects such as dry mouth, urinary retention, and blurred vision, and they may also cause sedation. Diarrhea and increased alertness are not the expected teaching priorities for this drug class.
source: Pulmonary study guide; antihistamine PowerPoint text; saved mixed quiz

stem: A client has a large pulmonary embolism. Which ventilation-perfusion pattern is most likely?
options: High V/Q ratio due to dead space
Low V/Q ratio due to shunt
correctAnswers: High V/Q ratio due to dead space
rationale: A pulmonary embolism blocks perfusion to ventilated alveoli, creating dead space and a high V/Q ratio. A low V/Q ratio occurs when perfusion is present but ventilation is reduced, as with shunt physiology.
source: Pulmonary study guide; ARDS/VQ PowerPoint text; saved practice exam

stem: A client with acute anxiety has ABG results: pH 7.55, PaCO2 27 mm Hg, and HCO3 24 mEq/L. Which acid-base imbalance should the nurse identify?
rationale: The pH is alkalotic and the PaCO2 is low, showing a respiratory cause. The bicarbonate is normal, so the best interpretation is uncompensated respiratory alkalosis, commonly seen with hyperventilation.
source: Renal study guide; acid-base PowerPoint text; saved renal and mixed quizzes

stem: Which findings are recognized risk factors for chronic kidney disease? Select all that apply.
rationale: Hypertension and diabetes mellitus are major CKD risk factors because they damage kidney blood vessels and filtering units over time. Exercise, low sodium intake, and hydration may be protective or supportive, not CKD risk factors.
source: Renal study guide; renal PowerPoint text; saved renal quiz

stem: A client is prescribed furosemide for fluid overload. Which teaching should the nurse prioritize?
options: Take the medication early in the day.
Increase potassium salt substitutes without checking with the provider.
Expect urine output to decrease after the dose.
Stop the medication when edema improves.
correctAnswers: Take the medication early in the day.
rationale: Loop diuretics increase urine output, so taking them early helps reduce nocturia and fall risk. The client should not self-stop the medication or add potassium without guidance because electrolyte changes are a key safety concern.
source: Renal study guide; fluid and diuretics PowerPoint text; saved mixed renal case

stem: Which factors are recognized causes or major contributors to peptic ulcer disease? Select all that apply.
rationale: Peptic ulcer disease is commonly associated with H. pylori, NSAID-related mucosal injury, and excess acid states such as Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. Hypertension and constipation are not primary causes of ulcer formation.
source: GI study guide; upper GI PowerPoint text; saved GI quiz

stem: Which factors increase a client's risk for constipation? Select all that apply.
rationale: Opioids slow GI motility, low fiber reduces stool bulk, immobility slows bowel activity, and obstruction can impair stool passage. Adequate fluid intake generally helps prevent constipation rather than causing it.
source: GI study guide; GI PowerPoint text; saved GI quiz

stem: A client with acute kidney injury has decreased erythropoietin production. Which CBC finding should the nurse expect?
options: Decreased white blood cell count only
rationale: Erythropoietin stimulates red blood cell production, so decreased erythropoietin can reduce RBC production and lower hemoglobin and hematocrit. Platelet or isolated WBC changes are not the expected direct result.
source: Coagulation/hematology study guide; anemia PowerPoint text; saved hematology quiz

stem: The nurse is monitoring a client at risk for disseminated intravascular coagulation. Which labs are most important to follow?
options: Platelet count, prothrombin time, and partial thromboplastin time
correctAnswers: Platelet count, prothrombin time, and partial thromboplastin time
rationale: DIC involves abnormal clotting and bleeding, so platelet count and coagulation studies such as PT and PTT are central monitoring labs. The other lab groupings may matter clinically but do not best track DIC.
source: Coagulation/hematology study guide; anemia/coagulopathy PowerPoint text; saved hematology quiz

stem: Which pathophysiologic change is central to type 1 diabetes mellitus?
options: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells causing insulin deficiency
Excess cortisol production causing insulin resistance
Overproduction of thyroid hormone increasing metabolism
Increased aldosterone secretion causing sodium retention
correctAnswers: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells causing insulin deficiency
rationale: Type 1 diabetes results from autoimmune beta-cell destruction, leading to absolute insulin deficiency and hyperglycemia. Cortisol excess, thyroid hormone excess, and aldosterone excess describe other endocrine disorders.
source: Endocrinology study guide; endocrine PowerPoint text

stem: A client with hypothyroidism is prescribed levothyroxine. Which outcome best indicates the medication is replacing the deficient hormone?
options: Improved energy and normalization of thyroid hormone levels
Immediate relief of acute chest pain
Rapid bronchodilation during an asthma attack
correctAnswers: Improved energy and normalization of thyroid hormone levels
rationale: Levothyroxine replaces deficient thyroid hormone in hypothyroidism, so improvement in hypothyroid symptoms and thyroid labs is the expected outcome. The other options describe effects of nitrates, bronchodilators, or diuretics.
source: Endocrinology study guide; endocrine PowerPoint text

stem: A client is prescribed an antibiotic and reports a history of a severe penicillin allergy. What is the nurse's priority action before administering the first dose?
options: Verify the allergy reaction and clarify whether the ordered antibiotic is safe to give.
Administer the dose because all antibiotic classes are unrelated to penicillin.
Hold all medications until the infection resolves.
Teach the client that allergies only matter with injectable antibiotics.
correctAnswers: Verify the allergy reaction and clarify whether the ordered antibiotic is safe to give.
rationale: The nurse should assess the allergy history and clarify safety before giving an antibiotic that may cross-react or be inappropriate. Antibiotic allergies can be clinically significant regardless of route, and treatment should not be stopped without provider direction.
source: Infection PowerPoint text; GI PowerPoint note on penicillin allergies; medication safety materials
